about: A 15-credit, Level 4 introduction to comparative politics, taken in Term 1 by first-year BSc Politics and International Relations students (and run in Term 2 for other programmes). The 2026/27 catalogue describes it as the study of domestic politics across countries: formal institutions, civil society, public attitudes and political culture and how they combine to shape political and policy outcomes, including the nature and development of states, democracy and dictatorship, and variation in democratic institutions. Its stated aims include an in-depth understanding of one country other than your own, a broad view of how political systems vary worldwide and how comparative methods answer descriptive and causal questions. Assessment is 40% coursework and 60% exam. The country-study topic gives a general framework because the specific country and readings are set by the module.
topics: Institutions, civil society and political culture
The comparative method and causal inference

notes.body:
Comparative politics is the study of domestic politics across countries. It asks why political systems differ and what difference the differences make: why some countries are democracies and others dictatorships, why some states are capable and others fragile, why party systems vary, and why similar policies succeed in one place and fail in another. It does this by systematic comparison, whether of a few cases in depth or many cases statistically.

Core concepts
- State: the territorial organisation claiming a monopoly of legitimate force (Weber, 1919).
- Nation: a community that sees itself as sharing an identity.
- Government: the people who currently hold executive office.
- Regime: the rules that determine how power is acquired and exercised, such as democracy or military rule. Regimes change more often than states.
- Political culture, civil society and institutions: the subject of the next topic.

Description and explanation
Two kinds of question run through the module. Descriptive questions ask what is the case (how democratic is country X, what type of party system?). Causal questions ask why (does proportional representation cause more parties?). Good descriptions require clear concepts and valid measures; good explanations need a credible mechanism and a design that rules out rival explanations.

Concepts and measurement
Giovanni Sartori (1970, "Concept Misformation in Comparative Politics") warned against conceptual stretching: extending a concept to many more cases by loosening its definition, so that it loses meaning. Arend Lijphart (1971) described comparison as one of the basic methods of science alongside the experimental and statistical methods, designed for situations with few cases.

How are regimes classified and measured? Three widely used sources:
- Freedom House's Freedom in the World rates political rights and civil liberties and labels countries Free, Partly Free or Not Free. Its 2026 edition (the 53rd, covering 2025, published in March 2026) reported a 20th consecutive year of net decline in global freedom, with 54 countries declining and 35 improving.
- The Polity project (Polity IV and Polity5) scores regimes on a scale from -10 (fully autocratic) to +10 (fully democratic); scores of 6 to 10 are conventionally treated as democracies and -10 to -6 as autocracies, with an intermediate "anocracy" zone. Check whether the series has been updated for the period you need.
- The Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) project at the University of Gothenburg uses thousands of expert ratings. Its Regimes of the World classification (Lührmann, Tannenberg and Lindberg, 2018) distinguishes closed autocracies, electoral autocracies, electoral democracies and liberal democracies. Its Democracy Report 2026 (covering 2025) counted 92 autocracies and 87 democracies among 179 countries, with 74 per cent of the world's population living in autocracies. These are figures at the time of writing (November 2026) and every annual report revises them, so check the latest edition.

Indices differ in definitions and methods, so countries near the boundary can be classified differently. When you cite a score, give the source and year.

Units and levels
Comparisons can be between countries, regions within countries, or across time. The choice of unit matters: national averages hide sub-national variation. Cases are never perfectly independent, either, because diffusion between countries (ideas, protest waves, policies) is common.

The aims of this module
You study a range of political systems and institutions, learn to explain differences and similarities, and examine at least one country in depth. Always ask what the country case illustrates about a general claim.

Exam tips: define your terms and state which source you use for classifications; do not present rankings as facts without noting how they are built.

notes.h: Institutions, civil society and political culture
notes.body:
Why do countries with similar economies have different politics? Three families of answers appear in comparative politics: institutions (the formal and informal rules), civil society (organised activity between the individual and the state) and political culture (shared attitudes and values).

Institutions
Douglass North (1990) defined institutions as the humanly devised constraints, "the rules of the game", that shape human interaction. In political science, institutions include constitutions, electoral laws, party systems, legislatures and courts. Gretchen Helmke and Steven Levitsky (2004) stress informal institutions: unwritten rules, such as clientelism, that are created and enforced outside official channels and can complement, compete with or substitute for formal rules.

Peter Hall and Rosemary Taylor (1996) described three "new institutionalisms":
- Rational choice institutionalism: institutions structure incentives and solve collective action problems.
- Historical institutionalism: institutions persist through path dependence, in which early choices create self-reinforcing patterns that are costly to reverse; critical junctures open windows for change.
- Sociological institutionalism: institutions shape identity and appropriateness (March and Olsen).

Civil society
Alexis de Tocqueville (Democracy in America, 1835 and 1840) argued that voluntary associations train citizens in self-government and check state power. Robert Putnam (Making Democracy Work, 1993) studied the regional governments created in Italy in 1970. Despite having the same formal institutions, the regions performed very differently, and he linked performance to long-standing traditions of civic engagement, horizontal networks and trust, which he called social capital. Bowling Alone (2000) argued that social capital declined in the United States. Critics question the direction of causation and the historical claims, and Sheri Berman (1997) showed that dense associational life in Weimar Germany was captured by the Nazi party, so civil society does not always support democracy.

Political culture
Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba (The Civic Culture, 1963) surveyed citizens in five countries (the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy and Mexico). They distinguished parochial, subject and participant orientations, and argued that stable democracy rests on a civic culture that mixes participant attitudes with deference and trust, not on participation alone. Ronald Inglehart (The Silent Revolution, 1977; Culture Shift, 1990) argued that, as societies become secure and wealthy, values shift from materialist to post-materialist. The World Values Survey, begun in 1981, supports comparative research on this. Inglehart and Christian Welzel (2005) linked value change with democratisation. Critics argue that culture may be a result of institutions as much as a cause, and that culture is too varied within countries to be a simple explanation, and warn against essentialising cultures.

Interaction
Institutions, civil society and culture interact. Institutions can create culture over time (citizens learn trust from fair institutions), and strong civil society can support institutions by monitoring government.

Exam tips: give authors and countries, specify causal direction, and say what evidence supports each argument.

States are the basic units of comparative politics, yet they differ enormously in capacity. Understanding how states formed explains much about why some can tax, regulate and provide security while others cannot.

What is state capacity?
Capacity is the ability to implement decisions across a territory. Commonly identified components are coercion (a monopoly of force), extraction (the ability to tax) and administration (a bureaucracy and rule of law). Max Weber's definition emphasises the monopoly of legitimate violence, and Michael Mann (1984) separated despotic power from infrastructural power, the capacity to penetrate society.

The European bellicist model
Charles Tilly argued that "war made the state, and the state made war" (1975), developing the thesis in Coercion, Capital, and European States (1990). Preparing for war required resources, so rulers built tax systems and bureaucracies, and the competitive pressure of interstate war favoured states that combined coercion and capital. Thomas Ertman (The Birth of the Leviathan, 1997) added that the timing of geopolitical competition and the existence of representative assemblies shaped patterns of state-building.

Other regions
- Latin America: Miguel Centeno (Blood and Debt, 2002) argued that wars in nineteenth-century Latin America were limited and did not build strong states.
- Sub-Saharan Africa: Jeffrey Herbst (States and Power in Africa, 2000) argued that low population density made it costly to broadcast power across territory, and that after independence the international community protected inherited borders, which reduced the pressure that interstate war created in Europe. Joel Migdal (Strong Societies and Weak States, 1988) showed how social organisations can resist state rules.
- Colonial legacies: Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson (2001) argued that where European settlers faced high mortality, colonisers established extractive institutions that persisted, whereas in healthier settler colonies they built institutions protecting property. Their evidence and instrument (settler mortality) have been disputed, so present it as a contested thesis.

Revolution and the state
Theda Skocpol (States and Social Revolutions, 1979) compared France, Russia and China and argued that revolutions followed state breakdown under international pressure combined with peasant revolts, and that they ended with stronger centralised states.

Nations and nationalism
State-building is related to nation-building. Benedict Anderson (Imagined Communities, 1983) argued that nations are imagined political communities, made possible by print capitalism. Ernest Gellner (1983) linked nationalism to industrial society's need for standardised education and culture. Eugen Weber (Peasants into Frenchmen, 1976) showed how schools, roads and conscription turned peasants into French citizens in the late nineteenth century.

Weak and fragile states
States that cannot secure a monopoly of force, collect taxes or provide basic services are often called weak or fragile (sometimes "failed", a contested term). Consequences include civil conflict, organised crime and dependence on external aid. Contemporary explanations include colonial borders, resource dependence, elite capture and weak accountability.

Exam tips: do not assume that the European path is universal; use at least one non-European example and mention the role of external actors and recognition.

A central task of comparative politics is classifying and explaining regimes. Debates concern the definition of democracy, the types of authoritarian regime, how regimes change and why they survive.

Defining democracy
- Minimalist or procedural: Joseph Schumpeter (1942) defined democracy as a method of choosing leaders through competitive elections. Adam Przeworski and colleagues (2000) operationalised it as a regime in which those who govern are selected through contested elections in which the opposition has a chance to win and take office.
- Robert Dahl (Polyarchy, 1971) added inclusive suffrage and civil liberties such as freedom of expression and association. His conditions involve contestation and inclusiveness.
- Liberal democracy adds protection of rights, rule of law and constraints on the executive. V-Dem distinguishes electoral democracy from liberal democracy on this basis.

Types of authoritarian regime
- Juan Linz (Totalitarian and Authoritarian Regimes, 1975; reissued 2000) distinguished totalitarian from authoritarian regimes by their degree of pluralism, ideology and mobilisation; Linz and Alfred Stepan (Problems of Democratic Transition and Consolidation, 1996) added post-totalitarian and sultanistic types.
- Barbara Geddes (1999) classified dictatorships by who rules: military, single-party and personalist regimes, and argued they differ in durability and in how they end. Personalist dictatorships often end in violent ways.
- Competitive authoritarianism: Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way (Competitive Authoritarianism, 2010) described regimes in which formal democratic institutions exist and are real arenas of competition, yet incumbents abuse state resources so heavily that the playing field is seriously skewed. Opposition can compete, and sometimes win, but unfairly. They argued that regime outcomes after the Cold War depended on linkage (ties to the West) and leverage (vulnerability to Western pressure), along with the strength of the ruling party or state.
- Andreas Schedler (2006) used electoral authoritarianism for regimes that hold multiparty elections without meeting democratic standards.

How dictators survive
Johannes Gerschewski (2013) identified three pillars of stability: repression, legitimation and co-optation. Jennifer Gandhi (2008) and others show that legislatures and parties help dictators co-opt elites and opponents. Milan Svolik (The Politics of Authoritarian Rule, 2012) emphasised two problems: preventing challenges from the masses (authoritarian control) and from insiders (power-sharing). Ronald Wintrobe (1998) pointed to the dictator's dilemma: repression undermines information.

Transitions and breakdown
Democratisation theories include modernisation (Lipset, 1959), class conflict models (Moore, 1966; Boix, 2003; Acemoglu and Robinson, 2006) and strategic interaction among elites (O'Donnell and Schmitter, 1986). Huntington (1991) described waves of democratisation. Linz and Stepan (1996) said democracy is consolidated when it becomes "the only game in town". Przeworski (1991) saw democracy as an equilibrium in which major groups find it in their interest to comply.

Backsliding
Nancy Bermeo (2016) described the shift from coups to executive aggrandisement, in which elected leaders gradually weaken checks on their power. Levitsky and Ziblatt (How Democracies Die, 2018) emphasise the erosion of norms of mutual toleration and forbearance. Annual indices point to a deteriorating global picture. At the time of writing (November 2026), Freedom House's Freedom in the World 2026 (covering 2025) reported 20 consecutive years of net decline, and V-Dem's Democracy Report 2026 (covering 2025) counted more autocracies than democracies (92 to 87). The numbers vary by index and are revised each year, so use the latest.

Exam tips: define democracy before classifying cases, and present data on global trends with source and date.

Democracies are not all alike. Comparative politics studies how institutional choices, especially the form of the executive, the electoral system and the distribution of power between levels and branches, shape representation, government stability and policy.

Executive-legislative relations
- Parliamentary: the government is chosen by, and responsible to, the legislature, which can remove it with a vote of no confidence. Heads of state are often ceremonial (a monarch or non-executive president), as in the UK and Germany.
- Presidential: a president, elected separately for a fixed term, heads the executive and cannot easily be removed by the legislature; the United States is the standard example. Juan Linz (1990) argued that such systems have dual democratic legitimacy and rigidity, increasing the risk of deadlock and breakdown. José Cheibub (2007) answered that breakdowns are better explained by other factors, such as the military's role and the type of country that adopts presidentialism.
- Semi-presidential: a directly elected president with considerable powers coexists with a prime minister and cabinet responsible to the legislature (Maurice Duverger, 1980). France's Fifth Republic (1958) is the standard example. Matthew Shugart and John Carey (1992) distinguished premier-presidential and president-parliamentary subtypes.

Electoral systems
- Plurality (first past the post) in single-member districts, as in UK general elections and US congressional elections.
- Majority systems, such as the alternative vote or two-round runoffs (France's presidential elections).
- Proportional representation (PR): party-list PR or the single transferable vote, designed so that seats approximate vote shares.
- Mixed systems: Germany's mixed-member proportional system, and the additional member system used for the Scottish Parliament (1999), combine local constituencies with a list tier.

Duverger (1951) distinguished two effects of plurality rule: the mechanical effect (small parties win fewer seats than votes) and the psychological effect (voters and donors desert hopeless candidates, and parties merge, anticipating the mechanical effect). Together they favour two-party competition, a tendency known as Duverger's law, while PR facilitates multi-party systems (Duverger's hypothesis). Gary Cox (1997) showed that in districts electing M members, strategic coordination leaves around M + 1 viable candidates. The effective number of parties (Laakso and Taagepera, 1979) is a measure of party system fragmentation. The Gallagher index measures disproportionality between votes and seats.

Majoritarian versus consensus democracy
Arend Lijphart (Patterns of Democracy, 1999; 36 democracies, 1945-96) contrasted:
- The majoritarian (Westminster) model: plurality elections, a two-party system, single-party majority cabinets, executive dominance, a unitary state and a single dominant chamber.
- The consensus model: PR, multi-party systems, coalition governments, balanced executive-legislative relations, federalism, bicameralism and often judicial review.
He argued that consensus democracies were no worse in managing the economy and were "kinder and gentler" on indicators such as representation and social policy. The finding has been challenged on data and methods.

Consociationalism
For deeply divided societies, Lijphart (1969, 1977) proposed consociational democracy with four features: grand coalition, mutual veto, proportionality and segmental autonomy. Critics note that it can entrench ethnic identities (Horowitz proposes incentives for cross-ethnic voting instead).

Veto players
George Tsebelis (2002) argued that policy stability increases with the number of veto players, their ideological distance and their internal cohesion.

Exam tips: always link an institution to a mechanism and evidence, and avoid saying PR is "better" without saying on what criterion (representation, accountability, stability).

This module pairs comparative themes with in-depth study of one country other than your own. The point of a country study is not to describe everything about it but to understand its politics well enough to test and refine general claims. This note provides a framework you can apply to any country; check your module materials for the specific country and readings.

A framework for analysing a country
1. Historical foundations: state formation, colonial or imperial legacies, critical junctures (independence, revolution, war, transition) and the path dependence they created.
2. Regime and constitution: where the country falls on classifications (V-Dem, Freedom House, Polity) and why; the constitution; the separation of powers; the role of courts, the military and the bureaucracy.
3. Executive and legislature: parliamentary, presidential or semi-presidential; the powers of each branch; policy-making processes and veto players.
4. Electoral and party systems: electoral rules, the effective number of parties, party organisation and funding, and the main lines of competition.
5. Society and cleavages: Seymour Martin Lipset and Stein Rokkan (1967) argued that European party systems reflect cleavages created by the National Revolution (centre versus periphery, state versus church) and the Industrial Revolution (land versus industry, owners versus workers), which then became "frozen". Other countries have other cleavages, such as ethnicity, religion, region or caste.
6. Civil society, media and political culture: associations, trade unions, trust in institutions, protest and public opinion (for example, from the World Values Survey or national election studies).
7. Territorial organisation: federal or unitary, the powers of regions and local government.
8. Economy and policy outcomes: economic structure, welfare provision, inequality, state capacity and how institutions shape policy.

Party systems
Giovanni Sartori (1976) classified party systems by number and ideological distance: one-party, hegemonic-party, predominant-party, two-party, limited pluralism, extreme pluralism and atomised systems. Hegemonic-party systems allow elections but not real competition, as in Mexico under the PRI for much of the twentieth century. Predominant-party systems involve genuine competition but one party wins repeatedly.

Using a country as a case
Cases play different roles in theory-building (Lijphart, 1971; Eckstein, 1975; Gerring, 2007):
- Typical or representative cases illustrate causal mechanisms.
- Crucial cases are those that must fit a theory if the theory is to be credible (or, for a least-likely case, that confirm it even under unfavourable conditions).
- Deviant cases do not fit predictions and so help generate new hypotheses.
- Comparative cases: a country can be compared with another to isolate factors.

Avoiding common mistakes
- Narrating rather than analysing: always link description to a question or a theory.
- Treating the country as unique: ask what is general and what is distinctive.
- Outdated information: politics changes; check recent events from reliable sources, and date any data you cite.
- Overreliance on one index: cross-check classifications.

Exam tips: in a country-focused answer, state the claim first, then use evidence from the country, and finish by saying what the case implies for the general argument.

notes.h: The comparative method and causal inference
notes.body:
Comparativists use systematic comparison to answer descriptive and causal questions. This topic covers the logic of the method, its limits and the main alternatives.

Mill's methods
John Stuart Mill (A System of Logic, 1843) proposed:
- The method of agreement: if cases share the same outcome and have only one factor in common, that factor may be the cause.
- The method of difference: if cases differ in outcome and are alike in all but one factor, that factor may be the cause.
Theda Skocpol (1979) used the method of agreement to compare the social revolutions in France, Russia and China, combined with the method of difference using contrasting cases such as Prussia and Japan. The methods assume a deterministic world with one cause, and they cannot handle several causes of the same outcome (equifinality) or interactions between causes.

Most similar and most different designs
Adam Przeworski and Henry Teune (1970) distinguished:
- Most similar systems design: choose cases that are similar on many background factors but differ in the outcome and the main variable of interest, so differences in other factors can be ruled out.
- Most different systems design: choose cases that differ on most features but share an outcome, looking for a common factor.
In practice no two countries are perfectly alike, so controls are partial.

The small-N problem
Lijphart (1971) identified the problem of "many variables, small N": there are more potential explanatory variables than cases, so many explanations fit the data. Remedies include increasing cases (within-country comparisons, over time), focusing comparisons on a few key variables, combining similar cases, or using other methods.

Fundamental problem of causal inference
Gary King, Robert Keohane and Sidney Verba (Designing Social Inquiry, 1994) argued that qualitative and quantitative research share a single logic of inference. Holland (1986) described the fundamental problem: we cannot observe the same unit with and without the cause. Responses are randomised experiments, natural experiments (Dunning, 2012), statistical controls and well-chosen comparisons.

Selection bias
Barbara Geddes (1990) showed that choosing cases on the dependent variable, for instance studying only countries that industrialised rapidly, can bias results because a pattern found among successes may also exist among failures. Selecting on the independent variable does not create the same bias (King, Keohane and Verba). Researchers should select cases to include variation in the outcome.

Process tracing and qualitative evidence
Process tracing examines the sequence of events and mechanisms linking cause and effect within a case (George and Bennett, 2005). Stephen Van Evera (1997) described tests of different strengths: a hoop test must be passed for a hypothesis to remain viable but passing does not confirm it; a smoking-gun test strongly confirms if passed but failing does not eliminate. This allows rich case evidence to support causal claims.

Set-theoretic and statistical approaches
Charles Ragin (The Comparative Method, 1987) developed qualitative comparative analysis (QCA), which treats causes as combinations of conditions that are necessary or sufficient for an outcome, accommodating multiple pathways. Large-N regression estimates average effects across many cases but depends on measurement and model assumptions. Many studies combine methods (mixed methods).

Exam tips: name the design you use and its weaknesses; discuss selection bias when choosing cases; and avoid claiming that a small-N comparison proves causation.

questions.q: Which set of categories is used by V-Dem's Regimes of the World classification?
options: Free, Partly Free and Not Free
Closed autocracy, electoral autocracy, electoral democracy and liberal democracy
Presidential, parliamentary and semi-presidential
Democracy, anocracy and autocracy on a scale from -10 to +10
questions.why: The four-way Regimes of the World classification is V-Dem's. Free, Partly Free and Not Free are Freedom House's labels. The -10 to +10 scale with an anocracy zone belongs to the Polity project. Presidential, parliamentary and semi-presidential describe constitutional forms of the executive, which are different from regime type.

questions.q: What does Sartori mean by 'conceptual stretching'?
options: Applying a theory to a later historical period
Applying a concept to more cases by loosening its definition, so it loses precision
Adding more countries to a sample to increase statistical power
Refusing to compare countries from different world regions
questions.why: Sartori warned that stretching a concept over more cases reduces its meaning. Increasing the sample is a design choice, not stretching. Refusing to compare across regions is an area-studies position that Sartori's argument does not require. Extending a theory in time is a question of generalisation, not of loosening definitions.

questions.q: Distinguish descriptive from causal questions in comparative politics, and explain why the choice of democracy index can matter.
markScheme: Descriptive: what is the case, classification
Causal: why, effect of X on Y
Measurement validity: concept and indicators
Different indices (Freedom House, Polity, V-Dem) differ in definition and method
Borderline cases classified differently; conclusions may change
questions.modelAnswer: Descriptive questions ask what the case is, for example how democratic a country is or what type of party system it has. Causal questions ask why, for example whether proportional representation produces more parties. Both depend on measurement, since a causal claim is only as good as the measure of the outcome and the cause. Democracy indices illustrate the issue. Freedom House labels countries Free, Partly Free or Not Free on the basis of political rights and civil liberties; Polity scores institutions on a -10 to +10 scale, with a middle zone of anocracy; V-Dem uses expert ratings to classify closed and electoral autocracies and electoral and liberal democracies. They define democracy differently and use different data and aggregation methods, so countries near boundaries may be classified differently, and a study of whether democracy causes growth might produce different results depending on the index. Researchers should therefore justify their measure and check whether results are robust to alternatives.

questions.q: What did Putnam's Making Democracy Work (1993) find about Italian regional governments?
options: Regions with more civic organisations performed worse
Regional performance was explained mainly by differences in current income
Regions with identical formal institutions performed differently, with civic traditions explaining the gap
Regions performed similarly because they shared the same formal institutions
questions.why: Putnam's point was that the same formal institutions produced different results, which he linked to civic engagement and social capital. Similar performance because of shared institutions is the reverse of his finding. Current income as the main explanation is a rival view; he argued that civic traditions predicted both performance and prosperity. More civic organisations performing worse is the opposite of his claim.

questions.q: What did Almond and Verba conclude in The Civic Culture (1963)?
options: Only a purely participant culture can sustain democracy
Stable democracy rests on a mix of participant attitudes with deference and trust
Social capital explains the quality of regional government in Italy
Values shift from materialist to post-materialist as societies get richer
questions.why: Their civic culture combines participation with deference and allegiance. The claim that only a purely participant culture sustains democracy is a misreading, since they emphasised balance. Social capital and Italian regions are Putnam's later study. The materialist to post-materialist shift is Inglehart's thesis.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by 'institutions' and distinguish formal from informal institutions, with an example of each.
markScheme: Defines institutions (North 1990) as rules of the game
Formal: written, officially enforced; example constitution/electoral law
Informal: unwritten, socially enforced; example clientelism
Helmke and Levitsky: informal institutions can complement, substitute or compete
Why it matters: same formal rules can have different effects
questions.modelAnswer: North (1990) defined institutions as the humanly devised rules of the game that constrain and structure interaction. Formal institutions are written and enforced through official channels, such as a constitution, electoral law or the rules of a legislature. Informal institutions are unwritten rules that are created, communicated and enforced outside official channels, such as norms of clientelism, in which votes are exchanged for favours. Helmke and Levitsky (2004) argue that informal rules may complement formal ones by filling gaps, substitute for them where they are ineffective, accommodate them by altering outcomes without breaking rules, or compete with them by contradicting them. This matters in comparison because the same formal institutions, such as electoral systems or regional governments, can produce different outcomes depending on informal practices, as in Putnam's Italian regions.

questions.q: According to Herbst (2000), why did many African states struggle to project power over their territories?
options: Africa lacked any form of pre-colonial political organisation
Ethnic diversity made it impossible for any state to form
Constant interstate war exhausted their resources
Low population density made it costly to broadcast power, and inherited borders were protected after independence, easing the pressure to consolidate
questions.why: Herbst's argument has two parts: the difficulty of projecting power over sparsely populated territory, and the international protection of borders, which reduced war-driven consolidation. Constant interstate war is the opposite of his claim, since the lack of such wars is part of his explanation. Ethnic diversity as an impossibility is not his argument. Pre-colonial states and polities existed in Africa, and his account does not deny this.

questions.q: What do Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001) argue about colonial institutions?
options: Where European settlers faced high mortality, extractive institutions were set up and persisted, affecting income today
British colonies always developed better institutions than French colonies
All colonisers created extractive institutions whatever the settlers' prospects
Tropical climates directly lower productivity regardless of institutions
questions.why: They argue that settler mortality shaped the kind of institutions colonisers built. The idea that climate directly reduces productivity is the geography hypothesis, which they contest. The claim that British colonies always did better than French ones is a coloniser-identity argument; AJR control for the identity of the coloniser and find that settler conditions, not the coloniser, drive the result. They claim variation depending on settlers' prospects, so the idea that all colonisers did the same is wrong.

questions.q: Compare Tilly's account of European state formation with explanations of state weakness elsewhere.
markScheme: Tilly: war, taxation, bureaucracy
Why this might not travel: Latin America (Centeno) limited wars
Africa (Herbst): density, borders, lack of interstate war
Colonial legacies (Acemoglu et al.) contested
Conclusion: European model not universal; context and external actors matter
questions.modelAnswer: Tilly (1990) argued that in early modern Europe competitive war-making drove rulers to extract resources and build administrative capacity, so that state formation was linked to war. Several scholars argue that this does not travel. Centeno (2002) claims that nineteenth-century wars in Latin America were short, limited and often fought by elites, so they did not stimulate lasting fiscal and administrative development. Herbst (2000) argues that in Africa low population density made it expensive to extend authority across territory, and that after independence the international community protected colonial borders, so interstate war was rare and states faced less pressure to consolidate. Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001) emphasise the legacy of colonial institutions, though their evidence is contested. Together these accounts suggest that the mechanisms that produced strong states in Europe depended on specific conditions, including frequent war, dense populations and competition between rulers, and that international recognition and colonial histories alter the path elsewhere.

questions.q: How do Levitsky and Way (2010) define competitive authoritarianism?
options: The military rules directly without any elections
Formal democratic institutions are real arenas of competition, but incumbents abuse state power so heavily that competition is unfair
A democracy in which the executive temporarily takes emergency powers
Elections are held but opposition parties are banned, so there is no real competition
questions.why: In competitive authoritarianism the opposition can compete and sometimes win, but against a skewed field. Regimes that ban opposition parties are closed or fully authoritarian, since there is no legal channel for real competition. Direct military rule is a different regime type in Geddes's classification. Temporary emergency powers describe a democracy under stress, not an authoritarian regime in which abuse is systematic.

questions.q: Which classification of dictatorships is associated with Geddes (1999)?
options: Presidential, parliamentary and semi-presidential regimes
Closed autocracy, electoral autocracy and electoral democracy
Totalitarian, authoritarian, post-totalitarian and sultanistic regimes
Military, single-party and personalist regimes
questions.why: Geddes classifies by the identity of the ruling group. The totalitarian, authoritarian, post-totalitarian and sultanistic scheme is Linz and Stepan's. The closed and electoral labels belong to V-Dem's Regimes of the World. Presidential, parliamentary and semi-presidential describe how the executive is organised in democracies, not types of dictatorship.

questions.q: Outline three ways in which authoritarian regimes try to survive.
markScheme: Repression: coercion, surveillance, but dictator's dilemma
Co-optation: parties, legislatures, patronage (Gandhi 2008)
Legitimation: ideology, performance, nationalism
Gerschewski's three pillars (2013)
Examples or limits: repression undermines information; coalitions of insiders (Svolik 2012)
questions.modelAnswer: Gerschewski (2013) identifies three pillars of autocratic stability. Repression includes surveillance, imprisonment and violence, which deters opposition, but Wintrobe (1998) notes the dictator's dilemma: repression makes citizens conceal their true preferences, so rulers lack information. Co-optation ties key elites and groups to the regime through patronage, party membership and institutions such as legislatures (Gandhi, 2008), giving them a stake in survival. Svolik (2012) shows that dictators must also manage the threat from insiders by creating credible power-sharing. Legitimation seeks active or passive consent through ideology, nationalism, economic performance or claims to represent the people. Regimes typically combine the three, and the balance varies: personalist regimes rely more on patronage and coercion, single-party regimes on organisation and co-optation.

questions.q: Which feature belongs to the majoritarian (Westminster) model in Lijphart's classification?
options: Coalition governments produced by proportional representation
A federal structure with a strong second chamber
Concentration of executive power in single-party majority cabinets
A grand coalition with mutual vetoes between segments
questions.why: Single-party majority cabinets concentrate power. Coalitions produced by PR are a feature of the consensus model. A federal structure with a strong second chamber also spreads power and belongs to the consensus model. A grand coalition with mutual vetoes is a defining element of consociational democracy, a related but different concept.

questions.q: Which of these defines a semi-presidential system?
options: A president who heads the government with a cabinet not responsible to the legislature
A directly elected president with significant powers alongside a prime minister responsible to the legislature
A president elected by the legislature who can be removed by it
A hereditary monarch as head of state with a prime minister
questions.why: The combination of a powerful directly elected president and a prime minister accountable to the assembly is the definition. A president chosen and removable by the legislature fits a parliamentary system with a ceremonial president. A hereditary monarch with a prime minister is a constitutional monarchy within a parliamentary system. A president heading the government with a cabinet not responsible to the legislature is pure presidentialism.

questions.q: Distinguish the mechanical and psychological effects in Duverger's account of plurality elections.
markScheme: Mechanical effect: seat allocation disadvantages small parties
Psychological effect: strategic voting and elite coordination
Both lead toward two-party competition under single-member plurality
Duverger's law as a tendency; Cox's M + 1
Exceptions: regionally concentrated parties (e.g. Canada, UK)
questions.modelAnswer: Duverger (1951) identified two effects that make plurality rule in single-member districts tend to produce two-party competition. The mechanical effect is that the electoral formula under-represents small parties: a party with 10 per cent of the vote spread evenly across districts may win few or no seats. The psychological effect arises because voters, expecting this, avoid wasting votes on hopeless candidates, and parties, activists and donors coordinate on the leading contenders or merge. Together they favour two parties, a tendency known as Duverger's law. Cox (1997) generalised the idea to M + 1 viable candidates in districts of magnitude M. The law is a tendency and has exceptions: regionally concentrated parties, such as nationalist parties in Canada or the UK, can win seats despite plurality rules, so the national party system may have more than two parties.

questions.q: Lipset and Rokkan (1967) explained European party systems through cleavages formed in which processes?
options: The Glorious Revolution and the American Revolution
The French Revolution and the Russian Revolution
The Reformation and the Enlightenment
The National Revolution and the Industrial Revolution
questions.why: Lipset and Rokkan identified cleavages arising from the National Revolution (centre versus periphery, state versus church) and the Industrial Revolution (land versus industry, owners versus workers). The French and Russian revolutions are political revolutions, though they influenced politics, and they are not their organising categories. The Reformation and Enlightenment are intellectual processes related to the state-church cleavage but not the two they name. The Glorious and American revolutions are not part of their scheme.

questions.q: In case-study methodology, what is a 'crucial case'?
options: The case with the most available data
A case in which the outcome of interest does not occur
A case chosen because it deviates from existing predictions
A case that must fit a theory if the theory is to be credible
questions.why: Eckstein's crucial case is a strong test: if a theory fails there, it is badly damaged. Choosing a case because it deviates from predictions describes a deviant case, whose purpose is to generate new hypotheses. Data availability is a practical consideration, not a methodological category. A case in which the outcome is absent is a negative case, useful for other purposes.

questions.q: Outline a framework for studying the politics of a single country and explain how the case could be used to test a general claim.
markScheme: Historical foundations and critical junctures
Regime, constitution and institutions (executive, legislature, courts)
Electoral and party systems, cleavages
Civil society, culture, economy and policy outcomes
Link to comparison: select what claim the case tests; typical, crucial or deviant case
questions.modelAnswer: A country study can be organised around history and critical junctures, the regime and constitution, the executive and legislature, the electoral and party system, social cleavages, civil society and political culture, territorial organisation, and the economy and policy outcomes. For example, one might ask whether the country's party system reflects the cleavages Lipset and Rokkan identified for Europe, or whether the electoral system produces the number of parties Duverger's law predicts. The case then serves a general claim: it could be a typical case that illustrates a mechanism, a crucial case that must fit the theory if the theory is to hold, or a deviant case that does not fit and so suggests missing factors. The analysis should state the claim first, use evidence from the country with dates and sources, and finish by saying what the case implies for the general argument and its limits, since a single case cannot establish a causal law.

questions.q: What characterises a 'most similar systems' design?
options: A random sample of many countries
Cases that differ on most features but share an outcome
Cases similar on many background features but different on the outcome and main variable of interest
A single case studied in great depth
questions.why: The most similar systems design holds background factors roughly constant to isolate the difference. Cases that differ widely but share an outcome describe the most different systems design. A random sample of many countries is a large-N statistical approach. A single case in depth is a case study, which may use process tracing but is not a comparison design.

questions.q: Why did Geddes (1990) warn against selecting cases on the dependent variable?
options: Qualitative methods cannot be used to study outcomes
Looking only at cases with the outcome cannot show whether the supposed cause is also present where the outcome is absent
Selecting on the independent variable always biases results more
Too many cases make qualitative analysis impossible
questions.why: If you study only cases with the outcome, a pattern found among them may also exist in cases without it, so inference is biased. King, Keohane and Verba argue that selecting on the independent variable does not produce the same bias, so the claim that selecting on the independent variable biases results more is wrong. Having many cases is a problem of resources, not of selection bias. Qualitative methods can study outcomes, but they require cases that vary.

questions.q: Explain process tracing and distinguish a 'hoop test' from a 'smoking-gun test'.
markScheme: Process tracing: evidence on the sequence/mechanism within a case
Used to test causal mechanisms, complement comparison
Hoop test: necessary but not sufficient; failing eliminates
Smoking-gun test: sufficient but not necessary; passing strongly confirms
Illustration or limits
questions.modelAnswer: Process tracing examines the events, decisions and mechanisms that link a supposed cause to an outcome within a single case, using evidence such as documents, interviews and timelines (George and Bennett, 2005). It helps decide whether a mechanism that comparison suggests actually operated. Van Evera (1997) classifies tests by their strength. A hoop test is necessary for a hypothesis to remain viable: if it fails, the hypothesis is eliminated, but passing does not confirm it much, because rival hypotheses may also pass. A smoking-gun test is sufficient: if the evidence is found, the hypothesis is strongly confirmed, but failing does not eliminate it since the evidence may simply be absent. For example, evidence that leaders had no access to a resource would be a hoop test for a hypothesis that they used it, whereas a leaked memo directly stating a plan would be a smoking gun. The method is limited by availability of evidence and risks of selective reading.

questions.q: 'What distinguishes democracy from dictatorship is that those in power can lose elections.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains the minimalist/procedural definition (Schumpeter; Przeworski et al. 2000)
Contrasts Dahl (contestation and inclusion) and liberal democracy (rights, rule of law)
Considers hybrid regimes: competitive authoritarianism (Levitsky and Way) and electoral authoritarianism (Schedler)
Evidence/measurement: V-Dem, Freedom House, Polity; dated figures
Discusses whether losing elections is sufficient or only necessary; backsliding
Considers alternative definitions and why the choice matters
Clear conclusion
questions.modelAnswer: The claim is the core of the minimalist or procedural view. Schumpeter (1942) defined democracy as a method in which leaders gain power by competing for votes, and Przeworski and colleagues (2000) turned this into a classification: a regime is democratic only if those who govern are selected through contested elections in which the opposition has a real chance of winning and taking office. The advantages are clarity and ease of measurement, and the test of alternation focuses on uncertainty of outcomes as the essence of democracy. However, there are reasons to think it is necessary but not sufficient. Dahl (1971) argued that polyarchy requires inclusiveness as well as contestation, with freedom of expression, alternative information and associational autonomy, since elections cannot be meaningful without them. Liberal conceptions add the rule of law, constraints on the executive and protection of minorities, so that an elected government that violates rights is not fully democratic; V-Dem distinguishes electoral from liberal democracy for this reason. Hybrid regimes show the difficulty. In competitive authoritarianism (Levitsky and Way, 2010), the opposition can compete and sometimes win, yet incumbents use state resources, media and the courts so heavily that the field is skewed. Whether incumbents 'can lose' is therefore a matter of degree, and the test of actual turnover can misclassify: a regime that has never lost may be a dictatorship or a dominant party in a fair system, as predominant-party cases suggest. The distinction also matters for measurement. Freedom House, Polity and V-Dem define democracy differently, so they classify borderline cases differently; at the time of writing (November 2026), V-Dem's Democracy Report 2026 (covering 2025) counted more autocracies than democracies among 179 countries (92 to 87), while Freedom House's Freedom in the World 2026 (covering 2025) reported a twentieth consecutive year of decline, and their numbers should be checked each year. Backsliding by elected leaders (Bermeo, 2016; Levitsky and Ziblatt, 2018) shows the weakness of a purely electoral test, because the process of eroding the ability to lose may happen gradually while elections continue. In conclusion, the ability of incumbents to lose elections is the best single criterion of democracy and underpins most definitions, but to be meaningful the elections must be free and fair, and this requires civil liberties and a level playing field, so the test is necessary but needs supplementing.

questions.q: Do electoral systems matter for the quality of democracy? Discuss with reference to Duverger and Lijphart.
markScheme: Describes electoral systems and mechanisms (plurality, PR, mixed)
Duverger: mechanical and psychological effects; Cox M + 1
Lijphart: majoritarian vs consensus; evidence on representation and performance
Criticisms and endogeneity: systems are chosen; other institutions; data issues
Defines 'quality' criteria: representation, accountability, stability, inclusion
Considers deeply divided societies: consociationalism vs alternatives
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer: Electoral systems translate votes into seats and so shape party systems, government formation and representation. The question is whether they affect the quality of democracy, which must be defined: key criteria are representation (do outcomes reflect voters' preferences?), accountability (can voters clearly reward or punish a government?), stability and inclusion of minorities. Duverger (1951) argued that plurality rule in single-member districts tends towards two-party competition because of a mechanical effect (small parties are under-rewarded) and a psychological effect (voters and elites desert hopeless candidates), while PR allows multi-party systems. Cox (1997) generalised this to M + 1 viable candidates in districts of M seats. Systems that produce two parties often provide clear accountability, since voters can replace the government with the main alternative, and single-party majority cabinets. But the cost is disproportionality: parties can win a majority of seats with a minority of votes, and many votes do not contribute to winning seats. PR gives more accurate representation, including for women and minorities, but coalition government can blur accountability because voters cannot be sure which parties will govern and the party that loses votes may stay in office. Lijphart (1999) examined 36 democracies and argued that consensus democracies, characterised by PR, coalitions and federalism, were as good as majoritarian ones at managing the economy and better on representation, equality and citizen satisfaction, so that they were 'kinder and gentler'. This has been criticised: the results depend on the countries and period, the concepts combine many features, and causal direction is unclear because electoral systems are chosen by actors in light of their interests. Other institutions and the social structure also matter; for example, plurality in a country with regionally concentrated parties may not generate two parties. In deeply divided societies, Lijphart's consociationalism recommends power-sharing, while Horowitz proposes vote-pooling incentives; each has risks and successes. Overall, electoral systems clearly affect party systems and representation, but their net effect on democratic quality depends on which criteria are prioritised and on the wider institutional and social context, so no system is best for all purposes.
